classification.difficultyReason: Combine two isosceles-triangle deductions with two applications of the exterior angle theorem to establish an angle identity.

content.prompt: Use the exterior angle theorem to prove that $\beta=3\alpha$ in the diagram below.

spec.description: Unlabelled triangle with horizontal base extended rightwards, vertical right side and an internal segment from a point on the sloping side to the lower-right vertex. Three matching double ticks are retained. Ordinary source blue linework becomes house black. Coordinates express the marked equal lengths; no numerical angle or right-angle mark is added.
spec.mathematics: The left-to-intermediate segment, intermediate-to-lower-right segment and right side have equal lengths. Alpha is the left interior angle; beta is the exterior angle between the right side and the rightward base extension. The intermediate point lies on the sloping side.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the source givens and angle symbols appear; vertex names and proof deductions are absent.

answer.short:
$\beta=3\alpha$.

Equal base angles in the two isosceles triangles, followed by the exterior angle theorem, give the result.
answer.worked:
Call the left vertex $A$, the lower-right vertex $B$, the upper-right vertex $C$ and the intermediate point on $AC$ $D$. The markings give $AD=DB=BC$.

Since $AD=DB$, the base angles of $\triangle ADB$ are equal, so $\angle ABD=\alpha$.

Using the exterior angle theorem in $\triangle ADB$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle BDC&=\angle DAB+\angle ABD\\\angle BDC&=\alpha+\alpha\\\angle BDC&=2\alpha.\end{align*}$$
Since $DB=BC$, the base angles of $\triangle DBC$ are equal. Thus $\angle BCD=\angle BDC=2\alpha$.

Using the exterior angle theorem in $\triangle ABC$,
$$\begin{align*}\beta&=\angle BAC+\angle ACB\\\beta&=\alpha+2\alpha\\\beta&=3\alpha.\end{align*}$$
